scales.name: Gong
scales.source: Jones, Stephen (1995). Folk Music of China: Living Instrumental Traditions. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
scales.description: The 'do'-mode of the five wusheng (five-tone) rotations of the anhemitonic pentatonic gong-diao system: gong-shang-jue-zhi-yu. Pitch-identical to the Western major pentatonic and to Korean p'yongjo built on this rotation.

scales.name: Shang
scales.source: Jones, Stephen (1995). Folk Music of China: Living Instrumental Traditions. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
scales.description: The second wusheng rotation, tonic on the shang degree of the gong-diao system.

scales.name: Jiao
scales.source: Jones, Stephen (1995). Folk Music of China: Living Instrumental Traditions. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
scales.description: The third wusheng rotation, tonic on the jiao degree of the gong-diao system.

scales.name: Zhi
scales.source: Jones, Stephen (1995). Folk Music of China: Living Instrumental Traditions. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
scales.description: The fourth wusheng rotation, tonic on the zhi degree of the gong-diao system. Korean court/folk p'yongjo mode uses this same pitch set, a consequence of Korea's import of the Chinese twelve-lu and pentatonic mode theory with Song-dynasty a-ak in 1116 CE, not coincidence. Also pitch-identical to the Japanese Yo scale below - see that entry.

scales.name: Yu
scales.source: Jones, Stephen (1995). Folk Music of China: Living Instrumental Traditions. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
scales.description: The fifth wusheng rotation, tonic on the yu degree of the gong-diao system. Pitch-identical to the Western minor pentatonic and to Korean kyemyonjo, the latter for the same historical-import reason noted on the Zhi entry.

scales.name: Gong (Pythagorean)
scales.source: Sanfen sunyi fa (three-part loss-and-gain method), the ancient Chinese stacked-fifths pitch-generation procedure attested in the Guanzi (4th c. BCE) and Lushi Chunqiu (239 BCE); see Service, Jonathan, 'Chinese Music Theory', Sounding China, Harvard University, https://soundingchina.fas.harvard.edu/Service.html
scales.description: True 3-limit stacked-fifths tuning of the Gong mode via the twelve-lu system (Huangzhong-Taicu-Guxian-Linzhong-Nanlu), rather than the 12-TET approximation above. At a 5-cent clustering tolerance this needs 2 pitch-bend channels; at 1 cent, 5.

scales.name: In
scales.source: Malm, William P. (1959). Japanese Music and Musical Instruments. Rutland, VT: Charles E. Tuttle.
scales.description: The miyako-bushi (urban) pentatonic of Koizumi's tetrachord theory, as presented by Malm. Pitch-identical to the Kumoi (Kumoijoshi) koto tuning below - shipped as a separate, explicitly named entry per this library's duplicate-collision policy, since the plan's own review flagged 'Hon Kumoi Joshi' vs In as an unlabeled-duplicate hazard.

scales.name: Yo
scales.source: Malm, William P. (1959). Japanese Music and Musical Instruments. Rutland, VT: Charles E. Tuttle.
scales.description: The ritsu (rural/folk) pentatonic of Koizumi's tetrachord theory, as presented by Malm. Pitch-identical to the Chinese Zhi mode above (both are the widespread 1-2-4-5-6 'suspended' pentatonic collection) - kept as a separate, explicitly cross-referenced entry rather than merged, since Yo and Zhi are independently named and sourced traditions.

scales.name: Hirajoshi
scales.source: Malm, William P. (1959). Japanese Music and Musical Instruments. Rutland, VT: Charles E. Tuttle.
scales.description: The living koto hirajoshi string tuning (1 2 b3 5 b6) as documented by Malm. A second, unrelated 'Hirajoshi' spelling circulates from Slonimsky's Thesaurus of Scales and Melodic Patterns (1947) - cents [0,100,500,600,1000] - which is pitch-identical to Iwato below; that variant is deliberately NOT used here to avoid an unlabeled duplicate, and is not shipped as its own entry.

scales.name: Iwato
scales.source: Malm, William P. (1959). Japanese Music and Musical Instruments. Rutland, VT: Charles E. Tuttle.
scales.description: A darker mode of the hirajoshi tuning family, described by Malm. Note this pitch set coincides with the Slonimsky-catalogued 'Hirajoshi' variant deliberately not used for the entry above.

scales.name: Kumoi (Kumoijoshi)
scales.source: Malm, William P. (1959). Japanese Music and Musical Instruments. Rutland, VT: Charles E. Tuttle.
scales.description: The kumoijoshi koto tuning (1 b2 4 5 b6), historically Yatsuhashi Kengyo's retuning of the hirajoshi family. Pitch-identical to the In entry above - a genuine, well-documented identity between two named traditions (koto tuning practice vs. Koizumi's miyako-bushi mode), not an authoring accident, so both are kept as separate, explicitly cross-referenced entries rather than merged or hidden.

scales.name: P'yongjo
scales.source: Lee, Hye-ku (1981). Essays on Korean Traditional Music (trans. Robert C. Provine). Seoul: Royal Asiatic Society, Korea Branch.
scales.description: The 'peaceful/bright' mode of Korean court and folk (sanjo) music, built hwang-tae-joong-rim-namu on the twelve-lu pitch set Korea adopted with Song-dynasty a-ak in 1116 CE. Pitch-identical to the Chinese Zhi mode above for that historical reason.

scales.name: Kyemyonjo
scales.source: Lee, Hye-ku (1981). Essays on Korean Traditional Music (trans. Robert C. Provine). Seoul: Royal Asiatic Society, Korea Branch.
scales.description: The 'plaintive/sorrowful' mode of Korean court and folk (sanjo) music, with the minor-third/major-second/major-second/minor-third interval pattern documented by Lee. Pitch-identical to the Chinese Yu mode above and to the Western minor pentatonic, for the same historical-import reason noted on the Zhi/P'yongjo entries.
